description: Turning real-world curiosity into a testable hypothesis and managing the practical constraints of an enquiry.
content_html:
From Curiosity to Question

Every statistical investigation begins with a question someone wants to answer. A teacher wonders whether students who sleep longer perform better in tests. A public health team asks whether exercise frequency is linked to reported wellbeing. A market researcher wants to know whether younger shoppers spend more online than older ones. In each case, the curiosity is real — but curiosity alone is not enough. Statistics demands that you turn your question into something testable.

A hypothesis is a precise, testable statement — not a vague hunch. Compare these two versions of the same idea:

  • Vague question: “Do students who sleep more do better?”
  • Testable hypothesis: “Students who sleep eight or more hours per night will score higher on a memory test than students who sleep fewer than eight hours.”

The second version names the variables, states a direction, and makes clear what data you would need to collect. That precision matters because your entire investigation — what data to gather, how to sample, which statistical tools to use, and how to judge whether your results support or refute your prediction — flows from the hypothesis you write at the start.

Key Fact

A testable hypothesis names the variables involved, states a predicted relationship or difference, and can be supported or refuted through data. The specification does not require formal null-hypothesis notation — a clearly worded statement is sufficient.

Why Hypotheses Can Only Be Tested Through Data

It is tempting to think that a well-reasoned argument can “prove” a hypothesis. Statistics says no. You can believe something is true for entirely logical reasons and still be wrong when the data is collected. A hypothesis can only be tested through the appropriate collection and analysis of data — this is a core principle of the specification. Opinion, intuition, and personal experience are starting points for forming a hypothesis, not evidence for evaluating one.

This is why the design of an investigation matters so much. If your data collection is flawed — biased sample, poorly worded questions, or measurement error — then your conclusion, however confidently stated, rests on shaky foundations.

Investigation Constraints

Real investigations face practical limits. The specification lists five main types of constraint you should be able to discuss: time constraints, cost constraints, ethical issues, confidentiality concerns, and convenience.

Time: A survey conducted over one week gives a very different result from one run over a full year. If you are studying seasonal behaviour — ice cream sales, flu cases, holiday bookings — and your budget only allows one month of data collection, your results may not reflect the full picture.

Cost: A large random sample is statistically ideal but expensive. Interviewing participants in person is richer than an online questionnaire but far costlier. Many investigators compromise on sample size or method because of limited funds, and this affects the conclusions they can draw.

Ethical issues: Investigations involving human participants must not cause harm, distress, or embarrassment. Researching sensitive topics — mental health, financial hardship, relationship difficulties — requires careful handling. Participants must give their consent, and the researcher must decide whether the benefit of the knowledge outweighs any risk of harm.

Confidentiality: Data collected about individuals must be protected. If people fear that their personal information will be shared or used against them, they may refuse to participate or give dishonest answers. Guaranteeing anonymity — not attaching names to responses — typically improves both response rates and honesty.

Convenience: Sometimes the ideal population is simply not accessible. A researcher wanting to survey a random sample of all UK secondary school students faces enormous logistical challenges. Convenience shapes who can realistically be included.

A research question asks something open-ended: “Is there a relationship between screen time and sleep quality?” That is a useful starting point, but it is not a hypothesis.

A hypothesis makes a specific, directional prediction: “Students who spend more than three hours on screens per evening will report fewer hours of sleep than students who spend less than one hour on screens.” Now you know exactly what to measure, how to group participants, and what a supporting result would look like.

In the exam, if a question asks you to “write a hypothesis” and you write a question instead, you will lose marks. Make sure your answer is a statement, not a question.

Proactive Strategies: Planning for Problems

Good investigators do not just hope that problems will not arise — they plan for them. The specification expects you to know what kinds of problems can occur during an enquiry and how to mitigate them before they happen. Three common challenges are: difficulty identifying the population, non-response, and unexpected outcomes.

Identifying the population: For some investigations, the population is easy to define — all Year 11 students in a school, for example. For others, the boundary is blurry. If you want to study “regular gym users”, what counts as regular? Once per week? Five times per week? Defining the population clearly before you begin prevents disputes about who should have been included later.

Non-response: If a large proportion of people choose not to respond to your questionnaire, the results may be biased. Those who respond might systematically differ from those who do not. For example, people with strong opinions tend to respond at higher rates than those with moderate views. Strategies to reduce non-response include: keeping questionnaires short, offering an incentive, and following up with reminders.

Unexpected outcomes: Real data surprises you. A value that seems impossibly large might be a genuine outlier, a data entry error, or evidence that your hypothesis needs refinement. A good investigator builds in a review stage rather than assuming everything will go to plan.

Key Fact

Proactive strategies — such as piloting the questionnaire, offering anonymity, defining the population precisely, and building in a follow-up for non-responders — reduce the risk that problems discovered later will invalidate the entire investigation.

A student wants to test whether students who travel more than 30 minutes to school are more likely to arrive late than those who travel fewer than 30 minutes.

Hypothesis: “Students with a commute of more than 30 minutes will have a higher rate of late arrivals than students with a commute of fewer than 30 minutes.”

Constraints identified:

  • Time — data collection limited to one half-term; seasonal effects (e.g. winter delays) not captured.
  • Ethical — lateness data is sensitive; consent needed from school and parents for under-16s.
  • Non-response — some students may not return the travel-time form; a follow-up reminder planned.
exam_tip_html: On ‘Explain’ and ‘Suggest and Justify’ questions about investigation design, always link your answer to the specific scenario in the question. Writing “it could be biased” scores nothing — you must say which group is under-represented and why that matters for the conclusion. For a hypothesis-writing question, check that your answer is a statement (not a question), names the variables, and states a direction or predicted difference. Missing any of these typically costs a mark.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • A hypothesis is a specific, testable statement predicting a relationship or difference between variables — it can only be confirmed or refuted through appropriate data collection and analysis, never by argument alone.
  • Real investigations face five main types of constraint: time, cost, ethical issues, confidentiality, and convenience — each can affect the sample size, method, and conclusions.
  • Proactive strategies — piloting, guaranteeing anonymity, defining the population precisely, and planning for non-response — reduce the risk of problems that invalidate an enquiry after data collection has begun.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is a testable hypothesis rather than a research question?
A) Does diet affect academic performance?
B) Students who eat breakfast every day will score higher on concentration tests than students who skip breakfast.
C) What is the relationship between exercise and mood?
D) There might be a link between sleep and exam results.
practice_questions.marks: B [1 mark] — Only option B is a specific, testable statement with named variables and a predicted direction.

practice_questions.text: A researcher wants to investigate whether students who cycle to school report higher levels of physical fitness than those who travel by bus. Give two constraints that could affect the design of this investigation.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark each for any two of the following, up to 2 marks:
- Time constraint: data collection at one point in the year may not reflect behaviour in winter months.
- Cost constraint: fitness assessments (e.g. measured tests) may be expensive; questionnaire-only alternatives are cheaper but less valid.
- Ethical constraint: asking participants about health or fitness may be sensitive; parental consent required for under-16s.
- Convenience constraint: the sample is limited to one school's students, so results may not generalise.
- Non-response: students may refuse to disclose travel method or fitness level.

practice_questions.text:
A student writes the following hypothesis for a statistical investigation: 'There is a relationship between the amount of revision a student does and their test score.'
Explain one way this hypothesis could be improved to make it more suitable for a statistical investigation.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 2 marks per developed point, up to 4 marks.
Mastering: Two distinct improvements, each with a clear reason linking to how the improvement makes the hypothesis testable.
- The hypothesis does not name a direction: a better version would state 'Students who revise more than 5 hours per week will score higher than those who revise fewer than 2 hours per week' — this tells the investigator what a supporting result looks like.
- 'Amount of revision' is not operationalised: a better version would specify hours per week, sessions per day, or similar measurable quantity — this makes the variable possible to collect consistently.
Secure: One developed improvement with a clear reason.
Developing: Identifies an improvement but the reason is vague (e.g. 'so it is clearer').
Emerging: Restates the hypothesis without identifying a genuine improvement.

practice_questions.text:
A health researcher wants to investigate the link between screen time and reported headache frequency in teenagers. She plans to post questionnaires to 500 randomly selected households and ask the parent to pass it to their teenage child.
Suggest and justify two proactive strategies she could use to reduce problems before data collection begins.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark for each valid strategy and 1 mark for a justification that refers to a specific problem it addresses, up to 5 marks total (one strategy may score 2 marks if the justification is developed).
Mastering: Two strategies, each with a justification linked to a named problem (non-response, sensitivity, measurement inconsistency, or population definition).
- Offer anonymity and emphasise confidentiality in the covering letter [1] because teenagers may under-report screen time or headache frequency if they fear their parents will see the results, which would bias the data towards lower values [1].
- Run a pilot study on a small group of 10–15 students [1] to identify whether the screen-time question is interpreted consistently — if students differ in whether they count passive TV watching, the variable will be measured differently across participants, introducing random error [1].
- Include a prepaid return envelope or online completion option [1] to reduce non-response, because households that do not return the questionnaire may include those with the highest screen time (who have less time for other activities), biasing the sample [1].
Secure: Two strategies with partial justifications.
Developing: One strategy with a justification, or two strategies without justifications.
Emerging: One strategy without a justification.

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between a research question and a hypothesis, using an example to illustrate your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 2 marks per developed point, up to 4 marks.
Mastering: Clear distinction with a specific example that illustrates both forms.
- A research question asks what the relationship might be (open-ended, e.g. 'Is there a link between exercise and mental health?') whereas a hypothesis is a specific, directional, testable statement (e.g. 'Students who exercise three or more times a week will report lower stress scores than those who exercise once or less per week') [2].
- The key feature of a hypothesis is that it specifies both variables and a predicted direction, so the investigator knows in advance what data would confirm or refute it [2].
Secure: Identifies the distinction with a partial example.
Developing: Identifies one feature without contrasting the two forms.
Emerging: Describes only one of the two forms.

practice_questions.text:
A student investigation team plan to study whether students in higher year groups spend more money per week than those in lower year groups. They decide to post their questionnaire on the school's social media page and analyse all responses received.
Discuss the limitations of this investigation design, including at least two different stages of the Statistical Enquiry Cycle.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for identified limitations with developed explanations, up to 6 marks.
Mastering: At least two distinct limitations at different SEC stages, each with a developed explanation of why it weakens the conclusions. A final evaluative comment addresses whether the results can be trusted.
- Hypothesis/planning stage: 'higher year groups' and 'lower year groups' are not operationalised — without specifying which years are being compared, the investigator cannot stratify the sample meaningfully [1+1].
- Data collection stage: posting on social media means only students who follow the page and choose to respond will complete the survey — this is opportunity sampling, not random sampling, so the sample is likely biased towards students who are more active on social media, potentially those who spend more money [1+1].
- Data processing stage: self-reported spending is prone to recall bias and social desirability bias — students may under- or overestimate weekly spend depending on what they think is expected [1+1].
- Evaluation: the combination of biased sampling and self-report measurement error means the conclusions about spending differences between year groups cannot be reliably generalised to all students [1].
Secure: Two limitations identified, one developed.
Developing: One limitation with partial development.
Emerging: Names a limitation without explanation.

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following best describes a hypothesis in statistics?
options: A question that asks what the researcher wants to find out
A specific, testable statement predicting a relationship or difference between variables
A summary of the data collected during an investigation
A conclusion drawn after analysing the results

knowledge_checks.q: Why might non-response bias an investigation into students' revision habits?
options: Because non-respondents will have identical revision habits to respondents
Because students who revise the most are the most likely to have time to respond
Because students who revise least may be less motivated to complete the questionnaire, making the sample unrepresentative
Because non-response only affects investigations with very large samples

knowledge_checks.q: A hypothesis can only be tested through the appropriate _____ and analysis of data.
Guaranteeing _____ in a questionnaire typically improves both response rates and the honesty of answers on sensitive topics.
Match each investigation constraint to its description:
right: Limited data collection period may miss seasonal patterns
The investigation must not cause harm or distress to participants
The ideal population may not all be realistically accessible

flashcard_questions.q: What is a hypothesis in statistics?
flashcard_questions.a: A specific, testable statement predicting a relationship or difference between variables.

flashcard_questions.q: Why can a hypothesis only be tested through data, not argument?
flashcard_questions.a: Logical reasoning can be wrong when evidence is collected; data alone supports or refutes the prediction.

flashcard_questions.q: A student writes 'Does sleep affect exam results?' as their hypothesis. What is wrong with this?
flashcard_questions.a: It is a question, not a statement. A hypothesis must be a directional, testable statement.

flashcard_questions.q: Name three main types of constraint an investigator may face when designing an enquiry.
flashcard_questions.a: Time, cost, and ethical constraints are three key types.

flashcard_questions.q: What is non-response in the context of a statistical investigation?
flashcard_questions.a: When some members of a sample do not complete or return the questionnaire, potentially biasing results.

flashcard_questions.q: How does guaranteeing anonymity help improve an investigation?
flashcard_questions.a: It encourages honest responses on sensitive topics and increases the response rate.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a proactive strategy in statistical enquiry planning?
flashcard_questions.a: A step taken before data collection to prevent or minimise a problem that could arise later.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is defining the population precisely important before data collection begins?
flashcard_questions.a: An unclear population boundary means it is disputed later who should have been included in the sample.

flashcard_questions.q: A researcher finds that only 20% of questionnaires are returned. What bias risk does this create?
flashcard_questions.a: Non-respondents may share a characteristic, making the results unrepresentative of the full population.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference between a time constraint and a cost constraint?
flashcard_questions.a: Time limits when data can be collected; cost limits the sample size or data collection method used.

glossary_terms.definition: A specific, testable statement that predicts a relationship or difference between variables, which can be supported or refuted through data collection and analysis.
A restriction on a statistical investigation caused by limited time available for data collection or analysis.
A restriction on a statistical investigation caused by limited financial resources, affecting sample size, equipment, or access to participants.
The situation where some members of a sample do not respond to a questionnaire or interview, which can introduce bias if non-respondents share a common characteristic.
